It opened on 5 December 2023 following the [[2023 New Zealand general election|14 October 2023 general election]], and dissolved on 1 October 2026 prior to the [[2026 New Zealand general election|2026 general election]]. The Parliament was elected using a [[mixed-member proportional representation]] (MMP) voting system. MPs represent 72 [[New Zealand electorates|geographical electorates]]: 16 in the [[South Island]], 49 in the [[North Island]] and 7 [[Māori electorates]]. The [[Electoral Act 1993]] provides for the remaining seats to be elected from [[Party lists in the 2023 New Zealand general election|party lists]] using the [[Sainte-Laguë method]] to realise proportionality to an expected total of at least 120 MPs.{{cite news |last=Wilson |first=Simon |date=14 September 2017 |title=MMP maths: How party vote percentages become seats in parliament |work=[[The Spinoff]] |url=https://thespinoff.co.nz/politics/14-09-2017/mmp-maths-how-party-vote-percentages-become-seats-in-parliament/ |access-date=10 October 2023}} Final results of the election determined that there are 123 members of Parliament, rather than the usual 120. 122 members were elected in the general election (there is an [[Overhang seat|overhang]] of two members for [[Te Pāti Māori]]).{{Cite web |title=Election 2023: Final results |url=https://interactives.stuff.co.nz/2023/election-2023-results-live/ |access-date=14 October 2023 |website=[[Stuff (website)|Stuff]] |language=en}}{{Cite web |date=14 October 2023 |title=2023 General Election – Preliminary Count |url=https://electionresults.govt.nz/ |access-date=15 October 2023 |website=Electoral Commission}} Due to the death of a candidate between the close of nominations and election day, [[Port Waikato (New Zealand electorate)|Port Waikato]] did not elect a representative and an additional list MP was elected to ensure Parliament would have at least 120 members. The 72nd electorate MP, and 123rd MP overall, was elected in the [[2023 Port Waikato by-election|Port Waikato by-election]] on 25 November 2023.{{cite news |last1=Cheng |first1=Derek |date=9 October 2023 |title=Election 2023: Act candidate Neil Christensen dies, by-election to be held for Port Waikato |work=[[The New Zealand Herald]] |url=https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/politics/election-2023-act-candidate-neil-christensen-dies/N2Z4P5MVKBAY5DJ7PDWLW27Y24/ |access-date=9 October 2023}} In May 2026 following Judith Collins appointment to President of the New Zealand Law Commission, she resigned her electorate seat which lowered the number of MPs to 122.{{Cite web |url=https://gazette.govt.nz/notice/id/2026-ps2600 |access-date=2026-08-28 |website=gazette.govt.nz |title=Notice of Vacancy in Seat in House of Representatives – 2026 }} Members in the 54th Parliament represent six [[List of political parties in New Zealand|political parties]]: [[New Zealand National Party|National]], [[ACT New Zealand]], [[New Zealand First]] parties, in [[Executive (government)|government]], and the [[New Zealand Labour Party|Labour Party]], [[Green Party of Aotearoa New Zealand|Green Party]], and Te Pāti Māori, in [[Parliamentary opposition|opposition]]. [[Christopher Luxon]] of the National Party formed a coalition government with ACT and New Zealand First and was sworn in as prime minister on 27 November 2023.{{Cite web |title=Coalition deal: Peters to be deputy prime minister first, followed by Seymour |url=https://www.1news.co.nz/2023/11/24/coalition-deal-peters-to-be-deputy-prime-minister-first-followed-by-seymour/ |access-date=24 November 2023 |website=1 News |language=en}}{{cite news |title=Christopher Luxon sworn in as New Zealand's new prime minister |url=https://www.1news.co.nz/2023/11/27/christopher-luxon-sworn-in-as-new-zealands-new-prime-minister/ |access-date=27 November 2023 |work=[[1News]] |publisher=TVNZ |date=27 November 2023}} == Background == === 2023 general election === {{main|2023 New Zealand general election}} The 2023 general election was held on 14 October. The opposition [[New Zealand National Party|National Party]] won 48 seats in the election, an increase of 14 seats. The ruling [[New Zealand Labour Party|Labour Party]] was reduced to 34 seats after losing a total of 28 seats. The [[Green Party of Aotearoa New Zealand|Green Party]], Labour's cooperation partner, got 15 seats, a rise of 6. The [[ACT New Zealand|ACT Party]] increased its seat count by one. [[Te Pāti Māori]] took five Maori seats from Labour, totaling six seats, one more than their party vote entitled them to, giving parliament a three-seat overhang. After being voted out in the [[2020 New Zealand general election]], [[New Zealand First]] returned to parliament, earning eight seats.{{cite web |url= https://archive.electionresults.govt.nz/electionresults_2023/|title= 2023 General Election – Official Result |website= ElectionResults.govt.nz |publisher= [[Electoral Commission (New Zealand)|Electoral Commission]] |date= 3 November 2023}} === Government formation === {{Main|Sixth National Government of New Zealand#Coalition negotiations}} Following the general election, the National Party required support from the ACT Party and New Zealand First to command the confidence of the House.{{Cite web |date=3 November 2023 |title=National and Act lose majority in final vote count |url=https://www.newsroom.co.nz/page/national-and-act-lose-majority-in-final-vote-count |access-date=3 November 2023 |website=Newsroom |language=en-AU}} Negotiations between the three parties took place after the official results were announced on 3 November. After three weeks of negotiations, [[Christopher Luxon]] announced the formation of a coalition government with ACT and New Zealand First on 24 November. On 27 November, Luxon was sworn in as prime minister by Governor-General [[Dame Cindy Kiro]]. == Parliamentary term == The final results of the election were announced on 3 November and the writ for the 2023 election was returned on 16 November 2023.{{Cite web |date=3 November 2023 |title=Official results for the 2023 General Election |url=https://elections.nz/media-and-news/2023/official-results-for-the-2023-general-election/ |access-date=19 November 2023 |website=Electoral Commission}}{{Cite web |date=16 November 2023 |title=2023 General Election writ returned |url=https://elections.nz/media-and-news/2023/2023-general-election-writ-returned/ |access-date=19 November 2023 |website=Electoral Commission}} Under section 19 of Constitution Act 1986, Parliament must meet no later than six weeks after this date; on 29 November 2023, following the new government's first Cabinet meeting, Leader of the House [[Chris Bishop]] confirmed that the Commission Opening and State Opening of Parliament would take place on 5 and 6 December 2023, respectively. === Timeline === *16 November 2023 – The writ for election is returned; officially declaring all elected members of the 54th Parliament.{{Cite web |date=16 November 2023 |title=2023 General Election writ returned |url=https://elections.nz/media-and-news/2023/2023-general-election-writ-returned/ |access-date=19 November 2023 |website=Electoral Commission |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250513040608/https://www.elections.nz/media-and-news/2023/2023-general-election-writ-returned/ |archive-date=13 May 2025|url-status=live}} *24 November 2023 – A coalition government is formed between [[New Zealand National Party|National]], [[ACT New Zealand|ACT]], and [[New Zealand First|NZ First]]. *27 November 2023 – [[Christopher Luxon]] is sworn in as [[Prime Minister of New Zealand]]. *5 December 2023 – The Governor-General issued the Commission of Opening of Parliament. ====Other ejections==== On 15 September 2026, Speaker Brownlee ordered Labour MP [[Ginny Andersen]] and [[ACT New Zealand|ACT]] leader [[David Seymour]] to leave the House of Representatives. Andersen had heckled National MP [[Carl Bates]] as he answered a question while Seymour had argued with the Speaker while questioning ACT MP [[Laura McClure]].{{cite news |last1=Gabel |first1=Julia |title=Speaker Gerry Brownlee boots two MPs from House within minutes |url=https://www.newstalkzb.co.nz/news/politics/speaker-gerry-brownlee-boots-two-mps-from-house-within-minutes/ |access-date=18 September 2026 |work=[[Newstalk ZB]] |date=15 September 2026}} On 17 September, [[Te Pāti Māori]] co-leader [[Debbie Ngarewa-Packer]] was ordered to leave the House after using the swear word "[[cunt]]" during an argument with Assistant Speaker [[Maureen Pugh]] during a debate on the National-led government's contentious move-on orders. Labour MP [[Willie Jackson (politician)|Willie Jackson]] was then ordered to leave after contesting Pugh's decision to discipline Ngarewa-Packer when the same word had previously been used in the House.
